job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mornings start at six because my little brother Mateo has school and our mum leaves for her cleaning shift. After that I'm at the kitchen table with my laptop, applying for graduate roles in electrical engineering. I finished my degree in June. In the afternoon I work on a small portfolio project, a battery monitor for solar panels, and I try to learn something new, usually a bit of Python or a PLC tutorial. By evening I'm cooking, because Mum is tired, and I look at job alerts again before bed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how has the job search gone since June?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Slowly. I've sent around sixty applications and got three interviews. One was for a grid-equipment company where my internship was, a ten-week placement testing transformers. They said they liked me but froze hiring. I have a good degree, but no money saved to speak of, and a big student loan that Mum can't help with. I'm doing some tutoring for school kids on Saturdays for pocket money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm relieved that the big promises were exaggerated, but it doesn't make my job hunt any easier. At the Saturday tutoring place I'd tell the other tutors that the work will still need people who understand how circuits and power actually behave. I'd also say that fresh graduates are being left to carry the cost of every slow year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau is just the world I live in now, and the world I live in is hard. There are few openings near our flat, and the ones that exist ask for two years of experience. I'd probably get something eventually, but I worry about the gap, and how much loan interest builds during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending applications, but I'd aim at contractors and installers who put in solar and heat pumps, because that work is growing whatever AI does. I'd finish my battery monitor and put it on a public repository so employers can see it. I'd also ask my old internship supervisor, Mr Okafor, if he knows anyone. And I'd keep tutoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. A low hum of worry, like a fridge you stop noticing until the power cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look if the grid-equipment firm stays frozen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, if the firm stays frozen I'd try the installers in the next town, even if the commute eats a third of the pay. I'd take a temporary job testing meters or doing inspections for a few months just to have a pay slip. Anything that is electrical and gets me through the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is helping you, and who isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Okafor helps, he reads my CV and sends me leads. My university's careers service is okay but quiet. What doesn't help is the system. Graduates are told to be flexible and cheerful while firms ask for experience they never provide. I think there should be more public funding for first jobs in green energy.

say: I'd say the hype faded but fresh graduates still carry the cost of **slow** hiring.
I'd tell other tutors power engineering will always need people who understand it.
think: A plateau is just today's hard world, and loan **interest** builds while I wait.
Local openings ask for two years of experience I can't get.
do: Aim applications at solar and heat pump **installers**, where work is growing anyway.
Finish my battery monitor and put it on a public repository.
Ask my old internship supervisor Mr Okafor for leads, and keep Saturday tutoring.
feel: A low **hum** of worry, like a fridge you only notice when the power cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need training, and we need it paid for. Software will take the paperwork, the drawings and the first-line checks, so juniors need new ways to learn on the job. I'd tell friends to start picking up automation and data skills now, not after they've been rejected twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it squeezes the exact jobs I'm applying for. A junior electrical engineer's first year is a lot of drawings, spec checking and test reports, and software does all that. But the site work and the testing stay human for longer, so I'm slightly more hopeful about the hands-on side of my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools properly instead of now and then, for the report writing and the circuit simulations. I'd add a short course in PLC programming and industrial controls, which firms still struggle to hire for. I'd apply for test and commissioning jobs, which are on site. And I'd ask my brother's school if I can run a small after-school coding club for pocket money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary but not frozen. It's like a river getting faster; I can still swim but I can't afford to waste time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of an electrical graduate's first year would software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing updates, the compliance paperwork, the standard calculations. At the transformer firm I spent days writing test reports that all looked the same, and I could see a program filling those in. The part where you stand next to a live panel and decide what's wrong is harder to hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change what you'd study next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd lean toward controls and automation, because someone has to set up and check the software that's replacing others. Maybe a part-time master's in a year or two, if the loan allows, but I won't sign up for more debt without a job lined up.

I'd tell friends to learn automation and data skills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to act, with income support, training money and rules on how fast firms can replace people. I'd say it publicly and I'd mean it. Nobody should have to learn to survive this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. Two years isn't long enough to land a first job, let alone build a career. By then thinking work is done better by machines, and my degree gets valued like a ticket to a train that's already left. The robot part comes later, but even the site jobs start changing once planning, ordering and scheduling are automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at getting on site-based work fast, because hands-on gets about three extra years. I'd ask for any apprenticeship-style job, even below my level. I'd cut my spending to the bone and try to keep two months of rent aside. I'd also join a group of recent graduates, because alone I'd be useless, and in a group someone knows something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold in the stomach. Not panic exactly, because I still have a plan, but close. It feels like the floor tilted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to Mateo, your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mateo that nothing's decided for him and that he should still study maths and things he's curious about. I'd say we'd look after each other, and I'd mean that more than I'd be able to explain. I'm the one who's supposed to be ahead of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of electrical engineering you'd count on holding up for 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the on-site part. Someone has to climb up and check a substation, and robots that do that well come around 2031, not 2028. So I'd bet on getting into that first. I'd rather be the person standing at the panel than the one in front of a screen when AGI arrives.

say: I'd say governments must act now with **income** support, training money and rules on speed.
Nobody should have to survive this alone.
think: Two years is too short to land a first job, and my degree could become a **ticket** to a train that's gone.
Even site jobs change once planning and ordering are automated.

Join a group of recent graduates to share leads and skills.

fieldNote: She turns fear into one concrete bet, getting to on-site work in the **three-year** gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough runway if people use it, so use it. I'd push for apprenticeship schemes and training funds, and I'd tell friends not to wait to see if it's really coming. Even if the date slips, learning controls and automation isn't wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the number that feels most real. It's long enough to get a first job, pay a bit off the loan and maybe change direction once, but short enough that I can't relax. If I land a job now, I'd have a few years of site experience before the thinking jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any electrical job that gets me on a real site, then study controls in the evenings. I'd put aside maybe a quarter of each pay cheque, and not renew my phone contract. After two years, I'd decide whether to specialise in grid maintenance or move toward energy storage. I'd keep tutoring because teaching might be a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of calm and nerves. Mostly steady, because I can see steps, but the feeling that I'm racing doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in the first year with five years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to stay near Mum and Mateo for the first year, because they depend on me being around. But I'd be more willing to move after that, if it's for a job in a place where the work is. Grid and storage sites aren't always in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still stay in the same town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be more careful with the loan. In the two-year picture I'd panic and spend nothing. Here, I'd budget so I can still eat and still save, because I need to last the whole race and not sprint the first lap and collapse.

I'd push for apprenticeships and training funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good moment to plan. At the tutoring job I'd tell students not to panic but to get skills that hold up, like understanding how things work, not just how to ask a machine. I'd tell my friends we have time to make sure it's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit more relaxed, though not carefree. Ten years lets me get a job, learn on site, maybe go back for a master's with an employer paying, and pay down the loan before things shake. But I'd still be around thirty-three when it lands, and I don't know whether my experience would count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it steady: first job, pay the loan, then professional registration, which most firms need for senior roles. I'd learn AI tools well, because the people who supervise them stay valuable. After five years, I'd rethink and maybe start a small solar installation business with someone I trust, if the market's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, honestly. There's still a knot, but it's the normal knot every graduate has. It's a better kind of worry than the other pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you do that you couldn't otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same thing I'd do now, only with more patience. A bad year of job searching wouldn't feel like the end of the world. And I'd put a bit of my pay into a pension early, which is boring but it would help with a ten-year plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your family anything different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell my mum she doesn't need to work nights forever, because in five years I could support her and my brother Mateo's studies. That's the thing I want most. I'd be careful about promising it, but I'd say it out loud.

We have time to make sure the change is fair.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too fast for Mum, for me and for Mateo's school years. What would help is boring and practical: paid first jobs for graduates, a pause on student loan payments while jobs are scarce, and training that connects to actual employers, not a certificate nobody reads. And someone to say what the plan is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say graduates are privileged because of the degree. I don't feel privileged. I feel like I'm holding a very expensive piece of paper while the rules change, and I'm still polite about it. I wish somebody would ask how we're paying for this period of waiting.

headlineQuote: I feel like I'm holding a very expensive piece of paper while the rules change, and I'm still polite about it.
portrait: Amira is a **23-year-old** electrical engineering graduate living with her mum and brother Mateo, with three interviews from sixty applications.
She has a good degree, a ten-week transformer-testing internship, heavy student debt and almost **no savings**.
She leans progressive and wants paid training, loan relief and public funding for green-energy first jobs.
Her adaptability is **steady**: she tries new tools once proven and bets on on-site work in the three-year gap.
Her moods stay anxious in most pictures, rise to alarmed with two years, and soften to uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most, because two years is too fast for her mum and brother, and for her.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **first jobs** for graduates, a pause on loan payments, and training tied to real employers.
